claims.passage: A Vela satellite recorded a light signal over the South Atlantic on 22 September 1979 that resembled signals associated with atmospheric nuclear explosions. An outside scientific panel could not determine whether it was nuclear. Its January 1980 findings preserve an unresolved assessment, not a verdict on every later argument.
claims.support: Supports the event and dated unresolved assessment.
claims.uncertainty: This is the panel's January 1980 conclusion, not a current universal verdict.
claims.followup: Compare later records before broadening scope.

claims.passage: The [declassified record](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1977-80v16/d368) contains two dated documents: Zbigniew Brzezinski's memorandum to President Carter on 9 January and the attached panel findings of 7 January. The attachment identifies satellite 6911 and distinguishes the signal's resemblance to known nuclear events from a discrepancy that raised doubt.
claims.locator: Document heading; Tab A heading and ¶1–2
claims.support: Identifies two dates, satellite 6911 and the signal discrepancy.
claims.uncertainty: No later assessment is represented by this document.
claims.followup: Retain precise dates when comparing assessments.

claims.passage: The panel considered ionospheric observations from the Arecibo radar in Puerto Rico suggestive, but ambiguous and insufficiently understood to corroborate a nuclear event. That is more specific than saying no other observations existed.
claims.support: Distinguishes suggestive Arecibo observations from persuasive corroboration.
claims.uncertainty: Ambiguity is the panel's assessment at that date.
claims.followup: Read original radar analysis before interpreting its signal independently.

claims.passage: It also considered sunlight reflected from a small meteoroid or satellite debris near the sensors. Computer modeling showed that a meteoroid with specified properties could produce the signal. A possible modeled mechanism is not evidence that the modeled object was actually present.
claims.support: Supports a modeled possible mechanism, not an observed causal object.
claims.uncertainty: No actual meteoroid detection is established here.
claims.followup: Obtain model methods and later analysis for quantitative claims.

claims.passage: The panel could not assign relative probabilities to the nuclear and natural explanations. That statement does not mean the alternatives had equal odds. It describes a limit on the assessment the panel was able to make.
claims.support: Panel could not assign relative probabilities.
claims.followup: Do not supply numerical probabilities without further evidence.

claims.passage: The panel recommended further searches for corroboration, statistical comparison of signals and review of meteoroid data. Its recommendations describe work still needed at that stage; they do not demonstrate what subsequent inquiries found.
claims.support: Supports recommendations rather than completed outcomes.
claims.uncertainty: No claim that the recommended work was subsequently performed.
claims.followup: Locate the subsequent records if describing outcomes.

claims.passage: A claim about responsibility would require additional evidence connecting an event to an actor. The January attachment does not provide that connection. Nor does the existence of an unresolved signal by itself establish concealment.
claims.support: Editorial inference: attachment lacks the event-to-actor evidence needed for attribution.
claims.uncertainty: Does not prove that no attribution evidence exists elsewhere.
claims.followup: Inspect specific attribution documents before adding actor claims.

reviews.changeSummary: Made recorder coverage and report date explicit; replaced general life-jacket wording with the report's particular observation and retained limits on comprehension, cabin preparation and individual fatality causation.
remainingReview: Confirm repository copy against the authoritative report and inspect relevant page images before adding disputed transcripts, exact timing or table-derived findings.
The reviewed life-jacket observations do not quantify a causal share of fatalities.
Assign a real author and obtain named human editorial approval, metadata approval, and release approval.

claims.passage: The Boeing 767 carrying Ethiopian Airlines Flight 961 exhausted its fuel and ditched near the Comoros on 23 November 1996. Of 175 people aboard, 125 died and 50 survived. Three hijackers had demanded Australia despite the crew's warnings about fuel.
claims.support: Supports event, hijacker demand and narrative totals; 50 survivors is 175 minus 125.
claims.uncertainty: Totals are from report narrative; no new visual table interpretation.
claims.followup: Check authoritative current report before publication.

claims.passage: The investigating committee attributed the accident to unlawful interference leading to fuel exhaustion. The hijackers' destination demand exceeded the aircraft's remaining capability. Coercion also obstructed the crew's attempts to manage the emergency as the fuel available for any response continued to diminish.
claims.support: Supports unlawful interference and fuel exhaustion causal chain.
claims.followup: Keep event cause distinct from individual fatality mechanisms.

claims.passage: The [Ethiopian Civil Aviation Authority's final report](https://www.fss.aero/accident-reports/dvdfiles/ET/1996-11-23-ET.pdf), dated 4 May 1998, says both flight recorders stopped before impact. Its cockpit voice recorder section also describes heavy distortion on the public-address and third-crew-member channel. The investigation therefore cannot be read as an uninterrupted recording of the final cockpit and cabin exchanges.
claims.support: Supports report date and gaps in recording coverage.
claims.uncertainty: OCR narrative inspected; no complete audiovisual reconstruction claimed.
claims.followup: Review authoritative copy and original recordings if exact final exchanges are needed.

claims.passage: In its flight history, the report describes the first officer finding some passengers with already inflated life jackets. He and cabin crew helped deflate them and demonstrated reinflation and bracing. The report says these instructions were given only in English and may not have been understood by some passengers.
claims.support: Supports reported inflation, crew assistance and possible language difficulty.
claims.uncertainty: Reported observation does not establish every passenger's action or comprehension.
claims.followup: Avoid enlarging this into a universal passenger-behavior account.

claims.passage: Those observations do not identify how many deaths, if any, resulted from premature inflation. They should not be expanded into a claim that every drowning, or a specified share of the fatalities, had that cause.
claims.support: Editorial limit: cited observations do not quantify deaths caused by early inflation.
claims.uncertainty: No assertion that early inflation caused zero deaths.
claims.followup: Require case-specific fatality evidence for a numerical causal claim.

claims.passage: The committee itself records difficulty evaluating cabin preparations with certainty under the unusual conditions. A responsible account should preserve that qualification. Advice about survival should not be improvised from a historical narrative, and a casualty should never be explained through an individual's supposed mistake without evidence.
claims.support: Preserves the report's stated difficulty evaluating preparation.
claims.uncertainty: Does not independently determine crew or individual passenger responsibility.
claims.followup: Retain qualification; do not improvise passenger safety guidance.

claims.passage: A Boston storage tank burst on 15 January 1919. NOAA's historical spill overview describes a tank holding at least 2.2 million gallons of molasses and reports 21 deaths and 150 injuries. These are attributed historical figures, not measurements made for this article.
claims.support: Supports date, tank contents and attributed reported toll.
claims.uncertainty: Later overview rather than original measurement or casualty ledger.
claims.followup: Trace precise totals to original records.

claims.passage: A [Boston Post report of 16 January 1919](https://www.massmoments.org/moment-details/great-molasses-flood/submoment/hugh-ogden-issues-report-on-cause-of-the-molasses-flood.html), reproduced in Mass Humanities' primary-source excerpt, counted eleven known dead at midnight. That was an early count, not the final toll. Its timing matters when comparing it with NOAA's later figure of 21.
claims.locator: Boston Post excerpt, third paragraph; NOAA A Sticky Mess
claims.support: Distinguishes midnight known-dead count from later reported total.
claims.uncertainty: Early count is provisional; no original scan inspected.
claims.followup: Verify original newspaper and casualty records.

claims.passage: The newspaper excerpt gave 2.3 million gallons. [Boston's Archives and Records Management overview](https://www.boston.gov/news/100-years-ago-today-molasses-crashes-through-bostons-north-end) also uses 2.3 million, while NOAA says at least 2.2 million. The lower-bound wording does not contradict the larger figure, but the sources do not establish an independently measured exact volume here. Converting one of those figures into more decimal places would add precision without resolving its evidentiary basis.
claims.locator: Post excerpt first paragraph; Boston opening; NOAA A Sticky Mess
claims.support: Shows reported values and lower-bound wording without inventing precision.
claims.uncertainty: Sources do not establish an independently measured exact volume here; gallon-unit conversion is not attempted.
claims.followup: Find primary tank inventory and measurement records before precise conversions.

claims.passage: The newspaper's account is evidence of what was reported immediately after the event. It should not be treated as a completed engineering investigation. Its dramatic descriptions of the wave require the same scrutiny as its provisional casualty count.
claims.locator: Primary Source excerpt as a whole
claims.support: Editorial distinction between early reporting and engineering evidence.
claims.uncertainty: Descriptive wave dimensions were not accepted as measurements.
claims.followup: Inspect original issue and engineering evidence before using dimensions.

claims.passage: A [2016 American Physical Society conference abstract](https://meetings-archive.aps.org/dfd/2016/l27/8/) by Nicole Sharp, Jordan Kennedy and Shmuel Rubinstein proposed examining temperature and the flow behavior of molasses. The abstract is a statement of research scope, not a complete engineering report with the methods and results needed to independently assess a failure reconstruction.
claims.support: Supports author identities and stated scope of research.
claims.uncertainty: A conference abstract is not a complete evidentiary basis for engineering attribution.
claims.followup: Obtain full methods and results before technical claims.

claims.passage: [NOAA's discussion](https://response.restoration.noaa.gov/about/media/molasses-and-other-weird-things-have-spilled.html) also calls fish deaths in Boston likely, while noting the lack of detailed documentation in 1919. That qualification should remain attached. Its discussion of a later Honolulu spill does not establish an identical Boston environmental outcome.
claims.locator: A Sticky Mess and opening Honolulu discussion
claims.support: Retains agency's likely qualifier and comparison limit.
claims.uncertainty: No measured Boston fish mortality is claimed.
claims.followup: Use Boston-specific environmental records before quantification.
